summary.text: A previously healthy 5-year-old boy was admitted to the pediatric emergency department with low-grade fever and a painful left cervical swelling since the day before, treated with paracetamol. On admission he was apyretic with normal vital signs, a hard elastic painful mobile cervical swelling of about 3 × 2 cm, and normal liver function tests.

Neck ultrasound showed enlarged lymph nodes, blood culture and SARS-CoV-2 PCR were negative, and intravenous ceftriaxone was started with rapid clinical improvement of the cervical lymphadenitis. Serology showed acute Epstein–Barr virus infection with persistently undetectable EBV-DNA; other infectious serologies were negative.

On day 3 he reported fatigue and asthenia and developed mild scleral jaundice and dark urine. Laboratory tests showed acute cholestatic hepatitis with transaminases more than 12 and 20 times the upper limit of normal, total bilirubin 2.4 mg/dl and gamma-GT 142 U/L. Hepatitis B, C and E serologies and antinuclear antibodies were negative, and ultrasound showed a minimally enlarged liver with normal parenchyma, a normal gallbladder and non-dilated biliary tracts.

With infectious and autoimmune causes excluded, ceftriaxone-induced hepatitis was diagnosed and the antibiotic was immediately suspended without replacement or other drugs; the RUCAM score of +6 made the drug relation probable. Biochemical data improved within a few days, with AST 58 U/L, ALT 118 U/L, gamma-GT 81 U/L and total bilirubin 0.94 mg/dl on day 10. A liver biopsy was judged unnecessary, no steroids were given, hemolytic anemia did not develop, and all liver function tests were below the upper limit of normal after 40 days.
